newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasuries threatened by mounting risks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries threatened by mounting risks.

text.p: U.S. government bond prices have surged since September but a long list of worries threatens to whittle away these gains in coming months, analysts said on Thursday.
With the peak Thanksgiving and Christmas buying season ready to roll, inflation could rear its ugly head.
Furthermore, the possibility of a yen recovery poses a liquidity risk, as the wall of capital from investors borrowing in yen at previously low interest rates would crumble away.

These factors will put upward pressure on bonf (Treasury) yields (thus pushing down prices) and could widen the 10-year yield spread between Treasury notes (T-bonds) and German government bonds (bunds) from its current 45 basis points (0.45 percentage points), analysts said.

"On a three month view, we've got the spread moving out to about 60 basis points on underperformance of the U.S.," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London. "That is based on our view that if we do get strong growth early next year the market will sell off," he said.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. bond was quoted at 100-12/32 at 1300 GMT in London, giving a yield of 6.471 percent, just off an eight-month low of 6.45 percent hit on Tuesday.
Treasury prices have climbed steadily and yields dropped since September as the U.S. economy slowed from its second quarter breakneck speed and inflation remained at bay.
Many analysts say Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has carefully nurtured this "Goldilocks" scenario, with the economy neither too hot, nor too cold, but just right.
The Fed's decision on Wednesday to keep interest rates on hold should allow the fairytale to continue, some say.
But others argue that the recently restrained but powerful U.S. consumer sector is set to spring into action with the approach of Thanksgiving on November 28 followed by Christmas.
Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking, expects fairly brisk sales, and said that will help the Treasury note/Bund gap to swell to 90 basis points by early next year.

"We have had a third quarter pause in consumer spending," he said. " That has left consumers in a much more comfortable financial position from the middle of the year when they were looking overstretched and overborrowed."
Yamaichi's Chester agreed. He said economic data were likely to be supportive until the end of the year.

October consumer and retail sales numbers released on Thursday were indeed subdued, but much of next year's interest rate policy hinges on the consumer and so will depend on holiday spending patterns.

Anaylsts said signs of yen gains could also begin to pose problems for Treasuries, although a recent attempt by the yen to push higher appears to have faded. T-bonds have been supported by a wall of Japanese money as investors borrowed in yen, taking advantage of extremely low interest rates.

"If the yen does appreciate significantly against the dollar from here and Japanese authorities are intent on adopting a stronger yen policy, then we could see signficant outflows of Japanese capital from U.S. Treasuries," said Chester.
Further ahead, budget shenanigans could also upset U.S. Treasuries, analysts said.

While Democrat President Bill Clinton appears to have recently eased his opposition to Republican proposals for a balanced budget amendment, the road to an agreement will be strewn with political and technical obstacles, analysts said.
"That is going to be the big thing for the Treasury market in 1997," said Lewis.
Chester said the key date for the budget will come when Clinton gives his State of the Union address and outlines formal proposals. Until then, speculation will swing the market.
David Bloom, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London, is not overtly negative on Treasuries but said investors should not be lulled into believing the Goldilocks story.
"There is a sense of complacency over the U.S. at the moment in that everyone is looking for a golden scenario and that Greenspan has achieved the perfect steady state," he said.
"Quite frankly from this type of levels you can get a surprise in either direction to shock the market," he said, also citing consumer spending as the possible spark.
